lessons.title: Washing, Peeling, and Cutting Fruits Efficiently
lessons.body: Start by washing all fruits in clean water with a small amount of food-grade sanitizer or a capful of bleach per 10 litres of water. Scrub firm fruits like mangoes and pineapples with a soft brush to remove dirt and pesticide residue. Rinse twice in clean water. For citrus, wash whole fruits before cutting to avoid contaminating the flesh. Peel mangoes with a sharp knife or a vegetable peeler, cutting away the skin in strips. For pineapple, slice off the top and bottom, stand it upright, and cut down the sides to remove the skin and eyes. Citrus can be peeled by hand or with a knife, but for juicing, you often cut them in half and squeeze without peeling. Cut fruits into uniform piecesâabout 2-3 cm cubesâso they blend evenly. Use a stainless steel knife and cutting board to avoid discoloration. Work in batches to prevent browning: as you cut, drop pieces into a bowl with a little lemon juice or ascorbic acid solution (1 teaspoon per litre of water). For large volumes, a mechanical slicer or a food processor with a slicing disc speeds up the job. Always keep your work area clean and wash tools between fruit types to avoid flavor mixing. Efficient prep means less waste and faster juicing. Aim to process 10 kg of fruit in 30 minutes once you are practiced. Remember: dull knives bruise fruit and reduce juice yield, so sharpen your knife every hour of work.

lessons.title: Juicing Mango, Pineapple, and Citrus: Step-by-Step
lessons.body: For mango juice, choose ripe but firm mangoes. Peel and cut the flesh away from the seed. Blend the flesh in a blender with a little water (about 1 cup water per 4 cups mango) until smooth. For a clearer juice, strain through a muslin cloth or fine sieve. If you want a thicker juice, skip straining. Add sugar to taste (start with 2 tablespoons per litre) and a pinch of citric acid or lemon juice to preserve color. For pineapple juice, peel and core the pineapple, then cut into chunks. Blend with water (1 cup water per 3 cups pineapple) and strain. Pineapple juice benefits from a quick pasteurization: heat to 80Â°C for 2 minutes, then cool quickly. For citrus juice, roll the fruit on a counter to soften, cut in half, and squeeze with a manual or electric citrus press. Strain out seeds and excess pulp. You can blend citrus segments for a pulpy juice, but avoid blending the white pithâit turns bitter. For all juices, taste and adjust sweetness. Store in clean bottles and refrigerate. If selling, pasteurize by heating to 75Â°C for 15 seconds, then hot-fill into sterilized bottles. Yield: 1 kg mango gives about 600 ml juice; 1 kg pineapple gives 500 ml; 1 kg oranges gives 400 ml. Always use food-grade equipment and keep everything clean.

lessons.title: Making Juice from Hibiscus (Zobo) and Baobab
lessons.body: Hibiscus (zobo) juice is made from dried hibiscus petals (roselle). For 5 litres of juice, use 200 g dried hibiscus. Rinse the petals in cold water, then soak in 5 litres of water for 4-6 hours or overnight. Boil the soaked petals and water for 15 minutes, then turn off heat and let steep for 30 minutes. Strain through a fine mesh or muslin cloth. Add sugar to taste (about 500 g for 5 litres), and optionally add flavorings: ginger (50 g grated), pineapple peels, or cloves. For a refreshing twist, add a teaspoon of vanilla extract. For baobab juice, use baobab fruit powder. Mix 100 g baobab powder with 1 litre of water and whisk until dissolved. Strain if needed. Baobab is naturally tangy and creamy; sweeten with honey or sugar (2-3 tablespoons per litre). You can blend baobab with hibiscus for a unique drink. Both juices should be pasteurized for longer shelf life: heat to 85Â°C for 5 minutes, then cool and bottle. Store in sterilized bottles in the fridge for up to 2 weeks. Without pasteurization, consume within 3 days. Hibiscus juice is rich in vitamin C and antioxidants; baobab is high in fiber and vitamin C. Always use clean water and sanitized equipment. For a sparkling version, add carbonated water just before serving.

lessons.title: Blending Fruit Combinations for Unique Flavors
lessons.body: Blending fruits creates balanced flavors and increases nutritional value. Start with a base juice that is mild, like apple, pear, or pineapple. Then add a flavor fruit: mango, passion fruit, or berries. For example, a classic African blend is mango-pineapple: 2 parts mango juice to 1 part pineapple juice. Add a squeeze of lime for brightness. Another popular mix is hibiscus-ginger with a splash of orange juice. When blending, consider acidity and sweetness. High-acid fruits (citrus, pineapple, hibiscus) pair well with sweet fruits (mango, banana, papaya). Avoid blending banana with citrusâit can become bitter. Use a ratio of 3:1 base to flavor for a subtle taste, or 1:1 for a bold blend. Always blend juices after they are extracted, not whole fruits, to control texture. For a smooth blend, combine juices in a large container and stir well. Taste and adjust: add sugar syrup (1 part sugar to 1 part water, boiled and cooled) for sweetness, or lemon juice for tartness. For a creamy blend, add coconut milk or yogurt. Popular African combinations: baobab-mango, hibiscus-pineapple, ginger-mango, and watermelon-lime. When selling, label the blend clearly and list ingredients. Keep blends refrigerated and sell within 3 days if unpasteurized. Experiment with local fruits like soursop, guava, and tamarind for unique flavors. Record your recipes so you can repeat successful blends.

lessons.title: Straining and Clarifying Juice for Smooth Texture
lessons.body: Straining removes pulp, seeds, and fiber to give a smooth mouthfeel. Use a fine-mesh sieve, muslin cloth, or a jelly bag. For clear juice, strain twice: first through a coarse sieve to remove large particles, then through a fine cloth. For citrus, a simple sieve works. For thicker juices like mango, you may need to press the pulp through with a spoon. To clarify further, let the juice sit in the fridge for 24 hours; sediment will settle at the bottom. Carefully pour off the clear juice without disturbing the sediment. You can also use a coffee filter for small batches. For large volumes, a wine press or a hydraulic press extracts more juice and yields clearer results. Another method is enzymatic clarification: add pectinase enzyme (available at brewing supply shops) at 0.1% of juice weight, keep at 40Â°C for 2 hours, then strain. This breaks down pectin and gives a clear juice. For most small-scale producers, simple straining is enough. After straining, pasteurize if you want shelf stability. Remember: the more you strain, the less fiber and nutrients, but the smoother the texture. For a cloudy juice (like orange juice), strain lightly to keep some pulp. Always sanitize your straining cloths and equipment to avoid spoilage. Store strained juice in clean bottles and refrigerate.

lessons.title: Handling Pulp: Waste or Value-Added Product?
lessons.body: Pulp is not wasteâit is a valuable by-product. After juicing, you are left with fruit pulp, peels, and seeds. These can be turned into additional products. Fruit pulp can be used to make jams, jellies, and fruit leather. For example, mango pulp can be cooked with sugar and lemon juice to make mango jam. Pineapple pulp can be used in cakes, muffins, or as a filling for pastries. Citrus pulp can be candied or used to make marmalade. Peels can be dried and ground into powder for flavoring or pectin extraction. Hibiscus pulp (from soaked petals) can be composted or fed to livestock. Baobab pulp is already a powder; the remaining fiber can be used in baking. To make fruit leather, spread pulp thinly on a baking sheet and dry in an oven at 60Â°C for 6-8 hours or in the sun. For jam, cook pulp with equal weight of sugar and a tablespoon of lemon juice per cup until thick. You can also sell pulp to bakeries or restaurants. Another option is to compost pulp for fertilizer. Never throw pulp awayâit can become an extra income stream. For example, a small juice business can sell mango pulp to a local bakery for 50% of the juice price. Always handle pulp hygienically and refrigerate if not used immediately. Drying or freezing extends its shelf life.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Juice Extraction and Processing Techniques

Module: Juice Extraction and Processing Techniques | Course: Fruit Juice & Concentrates

This practical reference gives African juice processors, small-scale agribusinesses, and food entrepreneurs a hands-on guide to the core techniques covered across the module. It focuses on what happens on the processing floor: how to wash, peel, and cut efficiently; how to juice mango, pineapple, and citrus; how to work with hibiscus (zobo) and baobab; how to blend, strain, and clarify; and how to turn pulp from a disposal cost into a revenue line. The emphasis throughout is commercial: yield, shelf life, food safety, and unit economics.

1. Washing, Peeling, and Cutting Fruits Efficiently

Preparation is where most small processors lose money. Poor washing, over-trimming, and inconsistent cutting reduce yield and introduce contamination. In African markets, where fruit may be purchased from open-air markets or aggregated from smallholder farms, the wash step is also a critical control point for dirt, insects, and microbial load.

Washing: Use potable water with 50â100 ppm free chlorine for a 2â5 minute contact time, followed by a clean water rinse. For mangoes and pineapples, scrub the skin with a soft brush. For citrus destined for peel oil or zest, wash thoroughly because the peel carries the essential oils and surface contaminants. Change wash water frequently; dirty water spreads contamination rather than removing it.

Peeling: Manual peeling with sharp stainless knives is common but labour-intensive. For mangoes, a mechanical or semi-mechanical peeler can raise recovery. For pineapples, top-and-tail first, then remove the rind in strips to minimise flesh loss. For citrus, avoid peeling if you plan to press whole fruit; instead, score and remove peel only when making marmalade or candied peel.

Cutting: Standardise cut size. Uniform pieces improve extraction efficiency and reduce the risk of over-blending, which can introduce bitterness from seeds and pith. For mango, cut cheeks away from the stone and dice. For pineapple, remove the core and cut into chunks. For citrus, halve or quarter depending on the press type.

Business tip: Track trimming loss as a percentage of purchased weight. A 5% improvement in recovery on 1 tonne of mango at $0.60/kg is $30 per tonne â meaningful at scale. Train staff on a standard cutting diagram and post it at the prep table.

2. Juicing Mango, Pineapple, and Citrus: Step-by-Step

Different fruits require different extraction methods. Using the wrong method wastes yield or damages flavour.

Mango: Mango is a soft, fibrous fruit. Use a pulper-finisher or a blender followed by pressing. Steps: wash, peel, destone, cut, blend or pulp, then press through a fine screen. Add ascorbic acid (0.05â0.1%) to slow browning. Mango juice is often blended with water, sugar, and citric acid to balance pH and taste.

Pineapple: Pineapple is juicy and fibrous. Use a screw press or hydraulic press. Steps: wash, top and tail, peel, remove eyes, core, cut, press, then strain. Pineapple juice benefits from quick heating (75â85Â°C for 15â30 seconds) to inactivate bromelain, which can cause bitterness and texture changes over time.

Citrus: Citrus is best extracted with a reamer or citrus press that avoids pressing the pith and seeds. Steps: wash, halve, press, strain, and optionally blend with other juices. For commercial scale, a citrus juicer with a rotating reamer and a strainer is efficient. Avoid excessive pressure on the peel, which releases bitter limonene and naringin.

Business tip: Match the press to the fruit. A single-screw press works well for pineapple and mango but can crush citrus seeds and pith. A dedicated citrus press reduces bitterness and improves yield per fruit.

3. Making Juice from Hibiscus (Zobo) and Baobab

Hibiscus and baobab are two of Africa's most commercially promising non-fruit juice ingredients. Both are widely available, culturally familiar, and have strong export potential.

Hibiscus (Zobo): The dried calyces are the raw material. Steps: sort and rinse calyces, soak or boil in water (typically 1:10 to 1:15 ratio by weight), steep for 20â40 minutes, strain, sweeten, and optionally add ginger, pineapple, or clove. For commercial production, pasteurise after bottling. Hibiscus juice is acidic (pH 2.5â3.5), which helps shelf life but requires corrosion-resistant equipment.

Baobab: Baobab fruit pulp is naturally dry and powdery. Steps: crack the hard shell, remove seeds and fibres, mill the pulp into powder, then reconstitute with water (typically 1:5 to 1:8). Baobab is high in vitamin C and pectin, so it thickens naturally. It blends well with mango, pineapple, and hibiscus. Because baobab is often wild-harvested, ensure supplier traceability and quality checks for aflatoxin and microbial load.

Business tip: Hibiscus and baobab have long shelf lives in dried form, which reduces storage risk. Process in batches and keep detailed records of raw material source, batch number, and yield.

4. Blending Fruit Combinations for Unique Flavors

Blending is where product differentiation happens. A good blend balances sweetness, acidity, aroma, colour, and mouthfeel. In African markets, popular combinations include mango-pineapple, hibiscus-pineapple, baobab-mango, and citrus-ginger.

Principles: Start with a base juice (60â70%), add a character juice (20â30%), and adjust with a small amount of acid, sugar, or spice (5â10%). Use a refractometer to measure Â°Brix and a pH meter to check acidity. Target pH below 4.0 for shelf-stable acidic juices. Avoid over-blending; too many flavours confuse the palate and complicate labelling.

Business tip: Develop three SKUs: a flagship blend, a value blend, and a premium blend. Test with local consumers before scaling. Keep a recipe card for every SKU with exact percentages and batch yields.

5. Straining and Clarifying Juice for Smooth Texture

Straining removes coarse pulp, seeds, and fibre. Clarifying removes fine suspended solids and produces a clear, premium product. Not all juices should be clarified; mango and baobab are often sold as cloudy juices, while citrus and hibiscus can be clarified for a cleaner look.

Straining: Use a stainless steel screen (0.5â1.0 mm) or a muslin cloth for small batches. For larger batches, use a pulper-finisher or a vibrating screen. Press the pulp to recover additional juice; do not discard it without evaluating its value.

Clarifying: Common methods include settling, centrifugation, filtration, and enzymatic treatment (pectinase). For small processors, settling followed by siphoning and fine filtration is practical. Enzymatic clarification with pectinase at 0.01â0.05% and 40â50Â°C for 1â2 hours can improve yield and clarity, but requires careful temperature control.

Business tip: Clarified juice commands a higher price in some markets but costs more to produce. Calculate the yield loss and energy cost before deciding to clarify.

6. Handling Pulp: Waste or Value-Added Product?

Pulp is not waste; it is a second product. Mango, pineapple, and citrus pulp can be converted into jam, fruit leather, animal feed, pectin, dietary fibre, or biogas. In many African cities, disposal costs are rising, so valorising pulp improves both profitability and environmental compliance.

Options: Dry pulp for fruit leather or flour; mix with sugar and acid for jam; feed to livestock after appropriate treatment; compost or digest for biogas. For citrus peel, extract essential oils or candied peel. For pineapple, use the core and peel for vinegar or animal feed.

Business tip: Quantify pulp output as a percentage of input. If pulp is 20â30% of fruit weight, a 1-tonne/day operation generates 200â300 kg of pulp daily. Even at low value, that is a revenue stream or a cost avoidance.

Sources: FAO, Fruit and Vegetable Processing (Bulletin 119); Codex Alimentarius CODEX STAN 247-2005; industry practice from African juice processors.

Sources: FAO, Utilization of Fruit and Vegetable Processing Waste; African Circular Economy Alliance case studies; IITA post-harvest handling guides.

â  SAFETY WARNING â FOOD SAFETY AND CHEMICAL HAZARDS

Never use untreated surface water for washing or dilution. Chlorine solutions must be prepared at the correct concentration (50â100 ppm free chlorine) and monitored with test strips; excessive chlorine leaves toxic residues. Pasteurisation must reach the required time-temperature combination (e.g., 75â85Â°C for 15â30 seconds for many juices) and be verified with a calibrated thermometer. Do not bottle juice in reused containers not designed for food; they can leach chemicals and harbour pathogens. If you use pectinase or other enzymes, follow the supplier's safety data sheet, store away from food, and label clearly. In all cases, maintain a clean water supply, handwashing stations, and pest control. When in doubt, discard the batch â a foodborne illness can destroy a young brand permanently.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Use potable water and sanitise all surfaces, knives, and presses before starting.
  • Measure and record input weight, output juice weight, and pulp weight for every batch.
  • Check pH and Â°Brix at blending and before packaging; target pH < 4.0 for shelf-stable acidic juices.
  • Pasteurise using a calibrated thermometer and timer; record time and temperature.
  • Label every batch with date, recipe code, and raw material supplier.
  • Evaluate pulp for valorisation before discarding; keep a pulp log.
  • Train staff on hygiene, knife safety, and standard cutting diagrams.
  • Review unit economics monthly: yield, energy, labour, packaging, and waste cost.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Fruit and Vegetable Processing (Agricultural Services Bulletin 119)
  • Codex Alimentarius â General Standard for Fruit Juices and Nectars (CODEX STAN 247-2005)
  • FAO â Utilization of Fruit and Vegetable Processing Waste
  • IITA â Post-harvest handling and food processing resources
  • WHO â Five Keys to Safer Food Manual

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentration of food-grade sanitizer for washing fruits?
options: A) 1 capful per 10 litres of water
B) 1 cup per 10 litres of water
C) 1 tablespoon per 1 litre of water
D) 1 teaspoon per 5 litres of water
quiz.explanation: A small amount of food-grade sanitizer or a capful of bleach per 10 litres is sufficient to sanitize without leaving harmful residues.

quiz.q: Why should you drop cut fruit pieces into lemon juice or ascorbic acid solution?
quiz.explanation: Lemon juice or ascorbic acid (vitamin C) slows enzymatic browning, keeping the fruit color appealing.

quiz.q: How many kilograms of fruit can a practiced worker process in 30 minutes?
quiz.explanation: With efficient prep, a target of 10 kg per 30 minutes is achievable.

quiz.q: What is the recommended water-to-mango ratio when blending mango juice?
options: A) 1 cup water per 4 cups mango
B) 1 cup water per 1 cup mango
C) 2 cups water per 1 cup mango
quiz.explanation: A ratio of 1 cup water to 4 cups mango gives a good consistency without being too watery.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid blending the white pith of citrus fruits?
options: A) It makes the juice too sweet
B) It turns the juice bitter
quiz.explanation: The white pith contains compounds that impart a bitter taste.

quiz.q: What is the approximate juice yield from 1 kg of oranges?
quiz.explanation: Oranges yield about 400 ml of juice per kilogram.

quiz.q: For pasteurizing pineapple juice, what temperature and time are recommended?
quiz.explanation: Heating to 80Â°C for 2 minutes pasteurizes without overcooking the juice.

quiz.q: How much dried hibiscus is needed for 5 litres of zobo juice?
quiz.explanation: 200 g of dried hibiscus petals is the standard for 5 litres of zobo.

quiz.q: What is the recommended soaking time for dried hibiscus before boiling?
quiz.explanation: Soaking for 4-6 hours or overnight helps extract flavor and color.

quiz.q: How much baobab powder is mixed with 1 litre of water for baobab juice?
quiz.explanation: 100 g of baobab powder per litre gives a good consistency and flavor.

quiz.q: What is the recommended pasteurization temperature and time for hibiscus and baobab juices?
quiz.explanation: Heating to 85Â°C for 5 minutes ensures safety and extends shelf life.

quiz.q: How long can unpasteurized hibiscus juice be stored in the fridge?
quiz.explanation: Without pasteurization, consume within 3 days for best quality and safety.

quiz.q: What is a good base juice for blending because of its mild flavor?
quiz.explanation: Apple juice has a mild, sweet flavor that blends well with stronger fruits.

quiz.q: Which fruit should you avoid blending with citrus because it can become bitter?
quiz.explanation: Banana can turn bitter when mixed with acidic citrus juices.

quiz.q: What is a common ratio of base juice to flavor juice for a subtle blend?
quiz.explanation: A 3:1 ratio of base to flavor gives a subtle taste of the flavor fruit.

quiz.q: What can you add to a fruit juice blend to make it creamy?
quiz.explanation: Coconut milk or yogurt adds creaminess to juice blends.

quiz.q: Which of these is a popular African fruit combination for juice?
quiz.explanation: Baobab-mango is a unique and popular blend in Africa.

quiz.q: What is the first step to clarify juice after initial straining?
options: B) Let it sit in the fridge for 24 hours
quiz.explanation: Refrigerating allows sediment to settle, making it easy to pour off clear juice.

quiz.q: What enzyme can be used to clarify juice by breaking down pectin?
quiz.explanation: Pectinase breaks down pectin, which helps clarify juice.

quiz.q: At what concentration is pectinase typically added for clarification?
quiz.explanation: A concentration of 0.1% of juice weight is standard for enzymatic clarification.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for straining juice to remove pulp?
quiz.explanation: Muslin cloth or a fine-mesh sieve effectively strains pulp.

quiz.q: What happens to fiber and nutrients when you strain juice heavily?
quiz.explanation: Straining removes pulp, which contains fiber and some nutrients, reducing them in the juice.

quiz.q: Which of these is a value-added product made from fruit pulp?
quiz.explanation: Pulp can be cooked with sugar to make jam, a value-added product.

quiz.q: How can you make fruit leather from pulp?
options: B) Spread pulp thinly and dry at 60Â°C for 6-8 hours
quiz.explanation: Drying a thin layer of pulp at low heat creates fruit leather.

quiz.q: What can be made from dried and ground citrus peels?
quiz.explanation: Dried citrus peels are a source of pectin, which can be ground into powder.

quiz.q: Why is it important to handle pulp hygienically?
options: A) To avoid spoilage and contamination
quiz.explanation: Pulp can spoil quickly and harbor bacteria if not handled properly.

quiz.q: What is a potential income stream from juice pulp?
quiz.explanation: Bakeries and restaurants may buy fruit pulp for baking and cooking.

quiz.q: How long should you boil hibiscus petals after soaking?
quiz.explanation: Boiling for 15 minutes extracts flavor without making it too bitter.

quiz.q: What is a good sweetener for baobab juice?
quiz.explanation: Honey or sugar can sweeten the tangy baobab juice.

quiz.q: What should you do to citrus fruits before squeezing to increase juice yield?
options: B) Roll them on a counter
quiz.explanation: Rolling citrus softens the fruit and breaks cell walls, making juicing easier.
